opus-5.5.text:
I think there were a few layers to it, and honestly a lot of it was pretty reasonable given what people knew at the time.

The first layer was intellectual. Behavior cloning had a bad reputation that went back decades. People knew the classic failure mode: you train a policy on expert demonstrations, it makes a small mistake, drifts into a state the expert never visited, and then the errors compound. There were theoretical results showing that the error can grow quadratically with the horizon. So for a lot of researchers, behavior cloning was the naive baseline you include to show your method is better, not something you'd build a research agenda on.

The second layer was cultural. At a place like DeepMind, reinforcement learning was a huge part of the identity. AlphaGo and the Atari results came out of the idea that an agent can discover behavior through trial and error, sometimes behavior that surpasses humans. Imitation learning felt philosophically limiting by comparison: you're capped by your demonstrator, so how do you get superhuman? There was also a sense that relying on human data didn't scale. The dream was that compute plus a reward function would do the work.

The third layer was practical. Collecting good robot demonstrations was painful. Teleoperation interfaces weren't great, the data was noisy and multimodal, and the models we had then couldn't represent that multimodality well. People would try BC, get a policy that averaged between two different ways of doing a task and did neither, and conclude the approach was fundamentally weak. Often it was the data and the model class that were the bottleneck.

What changed my mind, and eventually a lot of other people's, was seeing that many of those failures weren't inherent to learning from demonstrations. With more and better data, better teleop tools, and more expressive models that capture multimodal action distributions, behavior cloning went from a strawman to a surprisingly strong recipe. And on the robotics side, RL in the real world was itself very hard: reward design, safety, and the sheer number of samples were serious obstacles. So the practical comparison was never perfect RL versus flawed imitation. It was what actually gets a robot to do something useful.

I don't think the skeptics were wrong to be skeptical. The compounding error problem is real, and imitation alone won't get you everything. But I think the community underestimated how far you could push it, and how much of the problem was really a data problem in disguise.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning was central to DeepMind’s identity and frames imitation as philosophically limiting, identifying RL’s prominent status as a reason for resistance.

r002.rationale: It describes agents discovering behavior through trial and error, but does not clearly attribute a self-learning ideal to the robotics community.

r003.rationale: It says researchers felt reliance on human data did not scale and hoped compute plus a reward function would do the work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think you have to remember what the zeitgeist was at the time. This was maybe 2017, 2018, and reinforcement learning was really the dominant paradigm. DeepMind had just had these huge successes with Atari, with AlphaGo, and the whole framing of the field was that intelligence comes from an agent interacting with an environment, getting rewards, and improving through trial and error. Behavior cloning, from that perspective, looked almost embarrassingly simple. You collect some demonstrations, you fit a supervised model, and you're done. There's no exploration, no notion of optimality, and people would say, "Well, you're just copying the human, so at best you'll be as good as the human, and in practice you'll be worse."

And there was a real theoretical argument behind that too. The compounding error problem had been known for a long time. If your policy makes a small mistake, it drifts to states it never saw in the demonstrations, and then it makes bigger mistakes, and the whole thing falls apart. So there was this sense that behavior cloning was a known dead end, something you teach in the first week of an imitation learning class and then move on from. If you proposed a project built around it, the reaction was often, "Why would you do that? That doesn't scale."

I think there was also a cultural dimension. In a lot of the community, doing something that required collecting human demonstrations felt like cheating in a way. The elegant story was that the robot figures it out on its own. Relying on humans to show it what to do felt like a crutch, like you were sidestepping the actual hard problem.

What I think people underestimated was how much the picture changes once you have good models and enough data. A lot of the failure modes people associated with behavior cloning were really failures of small models trained on tiny datasets. When the policy is expressive enough to capture the multimodality in how humans actually do things, and when you have hundreds or thousands of demonstrations instead of twenty, the compounding error story becomes a lot less dramatic in practice. But that wasn't obvious at the time, and honestly it took a few years of people stubbornly pushing on it, and showing results on real robots, before the broader community came around.

r001.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning as the dominant paradigm at DeepMind, backed by major successes, and links that climate to skepticism about behavior cloning.

r002.rationale: It says the community valued robots figuring things out on their own and viewed human demonstrations as a crutch.

r003.rationale: It reports that behavior cloning was dismissed with the claim that it “doesn't scale,” tying that view to resistance.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the resistance came from a real limitation of behavior cloning: you’re learning from states an expert visited, but when you deploy the policy, it makes mistakes and ends up in states that weren’t in the demonstrations. Then it doesn’t know how to recover, and those errors compound. So there was a legitimate technical reason to be skeptical.

But there was also a question of what people considered the interesting research problem. If you think intelligence comes from learning through interaction, reinforcement learning feels like the fundamental solution. Behavior cloning can feel like you’re sidestepping that problem by having a human provide the answers.

I wouldn’t assume everyone at DeepMind had the same view. But in the wider robotics community, collecting demonstrations was also expensive, and it wasn’t obvious that scaling up that data would give you something general. So the disagreement was partly about the limitations of the method, and partly about whether imitation was a useful foundation or just a shortcut.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning seemed like a fundamental research problem, but does not attribute DeepMind’s suppression of behavior cloning to RL being its flagship agenda.

r002.rationale: It describes learning through interaction as a view some people might hold, but does not identify the robotics community’s ideal that robots should learn by themselves.

r003.rationale: It says it was not obvious that scaling up demonstration data would produce something general, expressing doubt that supervised behavior cloning could scale sufficiently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it came from the limitations people associated with behavior cloning. You train on demonstrations, but once the robot makes a mistake, it ends up in a situation that wasn’t in the training data. Then the errors compound. That’s a real problem, and it gave people a reason to think that simply copying demonstrations wouldn’t be enough.

There was also the appeal of reinforcement learning: the robot could discover a solution through experience, potentially doing something better than the person demonstrating it. Behavior cloning could seem less ambitious by comparison.

I think the important distinction is between saying behavior cloning has limitations and saying it isn’t a useful foundation. Learning from demonstrations gives you a starting point. You can then ask how to collect more useful data, recover from mistakes, and improve through interaction. Those approaches don’t have to be in opposition.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning appealed because robots could discover solutions through experience, but does not attribute DeepMind’s suppression of behavior cloning to RL being its flagship agenda.

r002.rationale: The response mentions learning through experience and improving through interaction, but does not identify a community ideal that robots should learn by themselves as a reason for resistance.

r003.rationale: It describes compounding errors when robots encounter situations outside the demonstrations, but does not say resistance came from a belief that supervised learning would not scale.
